correctness.rationale: For S=Z/4Z with shortest-cycle distance, unit-rate Poisson arrivals and unit-speed expanding closed balls, the tail of the first all-site cover time follows by inclusion-exclusion of all 15 nonempty target subsets. For a subset A, the Poisson void intensity has successive slopes a=mu(A), b=mu(B(A,1)),1 on the intervals [0,1],[1,2],[2,infinity); integrating gives I(a,b)=(1-e^-a)/a + e^-a(1-e^-b)/b + e^-a-b (continuous at a=0,b=0). Independent from-scratch subset enumeration recovers E_h=25/3-(32/3)e^-1/4+6e^-1/2-(4/3)e^-3/4-(4/3)e^-1 =2.544980946964... for uniform Haar h and E_nu=2+2e^-1/2-2e^-1=2.477302437082... for antipodal nu=(1/2,0,1/2,0). Independently, thinning gives first arrival at two supported sites as independent Exp(1/2), with C_nu=M+max(1,min(G,2)), M~Exp(1), G~Exp(1/2). Alternating exact rational Taylor bounds yield 0.0676785098698< E_h-E_nu <0.0676785099821. Thus Haar is strictly not optimal; there is no global optimizer claim. value.rationale: An elementary, exact, robust strict counterexample answers an explicit research question about Haar optimality in the general growing-ball model. It distinguishes the geometric group-invariance property from optimal center law. Even a four-point counterexample is valuable because it settles the unrestricted conjectural principle, without claiming connected-group behavior.

limitations: The finite metric group Z4 with zero seed mass at alternate sites is allowed; no assertion for connected compact groups, non-unit speed models, other n, or optimality among all mu.
residual_risks: An unindexed finite-group counterexample with the same Poisson growth law could predate this exact witness.
The comparison establishes strict improvement over Haar, not that the antipodal law is the global optimum or that connected groups behave similarly.
